lines: Clean feathers and straight shafts make trouble keep its distance.
A good bow is <pulse>ready</pulse> before the bell rings.
A crooked feather makes a promise the arrow can't keep.
Distance changes everything. Trouble looks smaller until it arrives.
The best warning gives us time to prepare.
Good aim takes a steady hand and the patience not to flinch.
Most days, I am at the fletching table, trying to keep straight shafts from becoming everyone else's problem.
Arrow making looks simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it becomes very important.
I trust a good knife more than a loud promise. The knife has less to prove.
Good arrows start with straight thinking and end with careful hands.
Feathers look light until the aim depends on them.
A bow tells the truth about tension very quickly.
The smallest flaw gets louder after release.
I measure twice because the arrow only flies once.
String, shaft, feather, point, and then the patience to check it again.
People think aim begins in the eye. It usually begins in the breath.
A village with arrows ready can sleep a little closer to peace.
Wind never hits an arrow the same way twice. That is why I keep checking the feathers.
A good fletcher respects distance without trusting it.
The straightest arrow still needs someone steady behind it.
I have learned more from missed shots than easy ones.
A crooked shaft is honest early. A crooked plan waits.
The target never moves, which is more than I can say for danger.
An arrow proves the work once it leaves the bow.
That route you took me on flew about as straight as a warped arrow.
My feet remember that road better than I do.
Next time, tell me how far we are going before I leave the village.
I kept expecting the next hill to be the last one. It never was.
The wind changed halfway there and I spent the rest of the walk guarding my spare string.
I should have packed more food and fewer things I never touched.
You found the way home, so I will give you that.
I learned where a full quiver starts feeling heavy.
There was one stretch of road so quiet I could hear my bow creak.
I watched your back out there. I hope you were watching mine.
The village gate was the best sight of the whole trip.
I know that route now, including every place I would rather not stop.
We crossed open ground with the wind against us and no cover worth naming.
I came home with sore feet and a much better sense of distance.
If we walk that way again, I want a map and a clear plan home.
I did not mind the miles. I minded not knowing how many were left.
The road taught me which gear belongs in my pack and which belongs on a shelf.
Some of that journey was worth seeing once.
You got me through the dangerous part without losing me. I remember that.
I will follow you again, but I am checking the weather first.
That boat did not fly straight, but at least it floated straight enough.
I still feel the water rocking when I stand still too long.
You never mentioned how cramped a bow feels in a little boat.
The current chose our route more often than either of us did.
I spent half that trip keeping spray off the feathers.
Next time, we bring a spare oar before a spare argument.
The shore looked close until we tried to reach it.
I learned that a full quiver makes a poor seat.
When the waves rose, every loose arrow started rolling at once.
You handled the boat better than I expected. Do not let that go to your head.
I was never so glad to step onto solid ground.
The fog swallowed both banks and left us following sound.
A wet bowstring can turn a bad crossing worse very quickly.
We made it home with the boat, the gear, and ourselves. That was enough.
If we take that waterway again, I want the wind behind us.
I could not tell whether the creaking came from the boat or my knees.
The river was quiet right before it became difficult.
I trusted you with the oars because I needed both hands on the gear.
That journey taught me to wrap spare strings twice.
I would travel by boat with you again after a long talk about the route.
A bowstring complains before it betrays you. Most people do the opposite.
Straight arrows are made from crooked material and stubborn hands.
When the bell rings, I learn which arrows were practice and which were promises.
Most days, I am at the fletching table, trying to keep straight shafts from becoming everyone else's problem.
Arrow making looks simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it becomes very important.
I trust a good knife more than a loud promise. The knife has less to prove.
One crooked feather can ruin an arrow. Of course I notice the little things.
The smallest flaw in a shaft is usually the one that ruins the whole job.
I can tell when someone rushed the work before they say a word.
Good fletching is mostly patience and knowing when to start over.
The weather changes how I work more than most people realize.
A sharp knife saves time, but a steady hand saves materials.
I learned this trade by making mistakes nobody lets me forget.
People only notice arrows when they need them immediately.
There is always one more repair waiting at the fletching table.
I would rather do a job slowly than explain a bad one twice.
You can judge a craftsperson by what they refuse to sell.
The busy days are easier than the days when nothing goes right.
I keep the useful scraps. Waste has a way of becoming valuable later.
Half this work is listening to what the wind is telling you.
